intro: A series converges when its partial sums settle on a number. Pick a series and add terms one at a time: the dots are the partial sums $S_n$, the bars the terms $a_n$, and the dashed line the sum when there is one. Below the picture, the six tests the AP® Calculus BC exam assesses, each marked for this series: which one settles it, and why the others cannot. Switch to Power series to drag $x$ along a number line and see where the series converges, endpoints included.
howItWorks:
Every partial sum is added up term by term in order, the way the definition says ($S_n = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n$). A picture of partial sums can suggest convergence but never prove it: $\sum \frac{1}{n \ln n}$ diverges, yet its partial sums stay under 3 for the first 500 million terms. That is why each series comes with the test that decides it, the condition the test needs, and its conclusion.

For a power series, the ratio test gives the open interval, $\lim \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| < 1$. At an endpoint that limit is exactly 1, so the ratio test cannot decide: each endpoint is a series of its own, tested with another test. In Test yourself the interval you type is graded in four parts (each endpoint and each bracket), so a missed endpoint is named.

The tests are the six in the course framework: the nth term test (divergence only), the integral test, direct and limit comparison, the alternating series test and the ratio test, with geometric and p-series as the series you compare with.
